title: Petrillo, records and the nightclub disc jockeys
summary: Saunders says the record industry and disc jockeys nearly ruined musicians; club disc jockeys at $30 a night shut bands out from about the early 1960s.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Well, Petrillo despite all his faults, did see the danger of records.
Yeah, right. When they had the strike back there, he fought that. And it was -- the disc jockey and the record industry has almost ruined the musician. They took
their own product and then just beat them across the head with it.
That's right. When did the night club disc jockeys come in on the South Side?
They have been in existence now about -- I would say, around -- in the early '60s.
Yeah, that's as I recall it.
I hadn't heard of that before.
No, no. But, see, what they would do is, when one guy is successful with one of the things, and monkey see, monkey does.
So these guys would get a guy and pay him $30 or $35 for a night, and he'd play these things, and the latest records, and they're so loud you couldn't hear, and they --
Right, right, talking and all that. So it became a fad. And so, that's just shut the musicians completely out.
